name: Bornholm Museum
label: Bornholm Museum
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/342991588: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bornholms Museum' (68 m across).
notes: The island's museum of cultural history, on Sankt Mortens Gade.

text.description: Bornholm Museum is the island's cultural history museum, and a good first stop in Rønne if you want to understand the place you are photographing. Inside, the story runs from the Palaeolithic to the present day. It includes the years of occupation during the Second World War, along with Bronze Age and Iron Age finds from the island. The museum association dates back to 1893, so this is an old institution with deep roots in the town. The same organisation looks after several other sites around Bornholm, including Erichsens Gård, the former Hjorths Fabrik terracotta factory and the citadel at Kastellet. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the building itself, seen as a calm, straightforward exterior shot that tells viewers where they are. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and wait for a gap if people or cars cross in front. If you want a closer detail, such as a doorway, a sign or a window, zoom in rather than walking right up to it. Entry and opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
text.geographic_location: In the town of Rønne on the island of Bornholm, Denmark.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Rønne and use the map to find the museum area. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit it all in, and use 2x for details such as the entrance or signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. This gives you enough distance to show the building as a whole.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them so the verticals stay straight. Leave a little space around the edges rather than cropping tight. Then take a second, closer shot of one detail with the zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a building like this, and a quiet moment helps keep people out of the frame. An overcast day also works well for even colour.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public space, but the museum itself may be ticketed with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Erichsens Gård
label: Erichsens Gård
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/342996983: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Erichsens Gård' (25 m across).
notes: Historic merchant's house on Store Torvegade, now a museum.

text.description:
Erichsens Gård is a timber-framed town house in Rønne, described as the town's best-preserved commoner's house, meaning an ordinary townsperson's home rather than a grand mansion. That is what makes it a pleasing subject: the painted timber frame, the low roofline and the old-fashioned proportions look just as a small-town Danish street used to look.

The house was built in 1806 and extended in the 1830s and 1840s. The architect Henning Pedersen lived here from 1816 to 1837. He designed Rønne Præstegård and the old city hall on Store Torv. The house takes its name from a later owner, Thomas Erichsen, who bought it in 1838. He and his wife had 12 children. One of them, Vilhelmine, became the muse of the artists Kristian Zahrtmann and Holger Drachmann. The house was protected in 1919 and sold to the Bornholm Museum in 1950. It still holds mementoes of those artists and an exhibition about the Erichsen family.

Use it for a wider scene that shows the house in its street. Then walk the couple of minutes towards it for close-ups of the timber frame, windows and doors. Keep your phone level, switch on the gridlines to keep the walls upright, and take a few frames at different distances. It is a small building, so you will not need to hurry.
text.geographic_location: Erichsens Gård is in Rønne on the island of Bornholm in Denmark. It is run as part of the Bornholm Museum.
text.directions_text: By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Erichsens Gård and get dropped nearby. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the house from a distance. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move right up to the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 95 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From where you stand, use the default lens (1x) to show the house with its surroundings, or zoom in to fill the frame with the roof and timber frame. Then walk about 2 minutes towards it for close frames of the timber, windows and doors. Turn on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the colours of the timber frame stay rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good choice, as the sun should be behind you when you face west. Overcast days also suit the muted colours of the house.

text.access_note: Erichsens Gård is part of the Bornholm Museum, so check the official site before you go to find out if you can go inside; you can photograph it from outside.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing east of the house and looking west, the morning sun is behind the photographer, so the view is front-lit.
Overcast light suits the muted colours of a painted timber-framed house.
The house can be photographed from outside, from the public street.
A taxi driver or scooter rider can find the house by name.

name: Rønne Theatre
label: Rønne Theatre
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/342941357: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rønne Theater' (18 m across).
notes: One of Denmark's oldest surviving provincial theatres.

text.description:
Rønne Theatre, also called Bornholms Teater, is a small half-timbered house painted yellow and brown, with a red tiled roof. It stands on the corner of Teaterstræde and Østergade, and it looks more like a cottage than a theatre. That is the charm of the photo: warm colours, dark timber lines and a steep roof.

The building dates from 1783 and was turned into a theatre in 1823. That makes it Denmark's oldest provincial theatre still in regular use. It has been a listed building since 1938, and it still stages plays, opera, cabaret and the annual Bornholmer Revue. Inside, the Baroque-style auditorium holds 302 people.

For a phone photo, the timber frame and the corner position do most of the work. Stand back so the whole corner fits, with the roof at the top and the street edge at the bottom. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole corner, try the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), but keep the building centred so the walls do not lean inwards. For a closer, tidier picture, switch to the default lens (1x) or step up to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) and pick out the timber pattern, windows or doors. If someone is walking past, wait a moment so the street looks calm.
text.geographic_location: Rønne Theatre is in Rønne, on Bornholm, on the corner of Teaterstræde and Østergade (East Street).
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Rønne and head for the corner of Østergade and Teaterstræde. Walk about 54 m west to reach it and look for the yellow and brown timber-framed house on the corner. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit the whole corner in, then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. A 2x telephoto, if your phone has one, suits details of the timber frame and doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the corner of the building up with one of the vertical lines so it does not lean. Keep the red roof near the top of the frame and leave a little street at the bottom. Hold the phone level and, if you can, step back a little before zooming rather than getting too close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Skip portrait mode: the building is flat and it makes the edges look odd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the colours and timber frame show up clearly; a bright overcast sky keeps the shadows soft. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the street; if you want to see inside or attend a performance, check the official site before you go.

name: St. Nicolas' Church
label: St. Nicolas' Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/115894199: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sankt Nicolaj Kirke' (53 m across).
notes: The main church in the town centre.

text.description: St. Nicolas' Church is the parish church of Rønne, standing near the harbour on the island of Bornholm. Its tower gives the town a strong landmark, and the building has a pleasing mix of old and later parts, which makes it a good subject for a phone photo. The site has a long history. A much smaller church known as Knuds Kirke stood here from about 1275, and some of its foundations can still be seen at the north-east corner. Around 1350 the church was extended westwards until it was almost twice as long. The tower was first added in 1550 and rebuilt in 1699. The last big changes came between 1915 and 1918, when the church was widened and given a southern transept, with the aim of keeping the original style. Inside, the altar was carved by Christian Kofoed in 1918, and the painting above it, showing Jesus calming the storm, is by Sven Havsteen Mikkelsen. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit in the full height of the building, and keep your phone level so the walls and tower do not lean. If you want a tighter picture of the tower, step back as far as you comfortably can and use the telephoto lens.
text.geographic_location: St. Nicolas' Church is the parish church of Rønne on the island of Bornholm, and it stands near the harbour.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the harbour area in Rønne, where the church stands nearby, and walk to the church. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), because you are close to the building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the walls, or the telephoto lens (2x-5x) for the tower and roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The church fills the view in front of you, with the tower a little to one side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it stays upright. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level. Try one wide shot with some pavement or sky around the church, then a close one using the telephoto lens that picks out the tower and the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky does not wash out. If the phone offers an HDR or Live Photo option, leave it on for steadier results in mixed light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around midday or in the early afternoon, when the south side you are facing is likely to be well lit. Early morning or evening gives a softer, warmer light, but the front may then be in shade.

text.access_note: St. Nicolas' Church is a working parish church, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules about going inside.

name: Rønne Lighthouse
label: Rønne Lighthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Havnebakken' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Havnebakken nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/735297525: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rønne Fyr' (6 m across).

text.description:
Rønne Lighthouse, also known locally as Rønne Bagfyr, is a slim white tower between houses, close to the waterfront in Rønne. It was built in 1880 by the Bornholm firm H. Wichmann & Co. It is made of cast iron, with an eight-sided tapering body, a gallery round the top and a green lantern dome. In all it is 18 metres tall. It was restored and repainted in 2000, and it no longer works as a lighthouse, having been taken out of service in the late 1980s.

It photographs well because it doesn't stand on its own. It sits between ordinary houses, a little back from the water, so you can show the tower rising above the street and the roofs on the slope, with the harbour basin below. The white paint and green top stand out against the surrounding buildings, and the shape is simple enough to read clearly even in a small phone picture.

The photo on this map is taken from Havnebakken, the street the tower stands on. It is a calmer, street-level view than standing right at the foot of the tower. Keep the tower upright in the frame and let the houses and the harbour tell you where you are. The tower is not open inside, so this is a photo-from-outside stop. If you want the tower close up, or a wider look down over the harbour basin, try the other viewpoints mentioned in the framing advice below.
text.geographic_location: In the old harbour district of Rønne, on Havnebakken, on the slope just back from the harbour basin and among the town houses.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot. Head for the harbour area in the centre of Rønne. The tower is then about 1 minute on foot to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower, the street and the houses in one frame. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the lantern and gallery. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of the street, and keep the phone level, as it can make the tower look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Havnebakken. The lighthouse rising above the street and houses on the slope, with the harbour basin visible below. From here the lighthouse is to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Leave some street and rooftops in the lower part of the frame to give the tower a sense of scale. For a different view, the tower can also be seen close up from the hill above the harbour, and a Kapelvej view looks down over the harbour basin. Check the Kapelvej view on the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the white paint looks washed out against the sky. Take the shot in portrait orientation to fit the full height of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters white paint and gives more shape to the cast-iron detail. Early in the day, the street is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The photo is taken from a public street, but the tower itself is not open inside; check the official site before you go if you want to know about any access to the tower.
